questions.prompt: Create a class `Student` with a constructor that takes name, course, and score. Add a method `getGrade()` that returns 'A' (>=80), 'B' (>=60), 'C' (>=50), or 'F'. Add a method `getSummary()` that returns: 'Amara — JavaScript — A'. Create two instances and print their summaries.

Create a class `BankAccount` with a private field `#balance`. The constructor takes ownerName and initialBalance. Add a getter `balance` that returns the value. Add a setter `balance` that throws an error if the value is negative. Add a method `deposit(amount)` that adds to the balance. Create an instance, deposit ₦5000, then log the balance. Try setting balance to -100 inside a try/catch and log the error message.
What is the purpose of private fields (#) in JavaScript classes? Why not just use regular properties?
questions.sample_answer: Private fields (prefixed with #) are only accessible inside the class body — code outside the class cannot read or write them directly. Regular properties are fully accessible from anywhere. Purpose: (1) Encapsulation — you protect internal state from accidental or invalid modification. A #balance field forces all changes to go through methods or setters that can validate the input. (2) API clarity — public properties are the intended interface; private fields are implementation details that can change without breaking external code. Without private fields, any code could do `account.balance = -99999` and bypass all validation. With #balance, the only way to change it is through the setter or methods you define — you control the rules.

Create a class `Counter` with a static property `total` starting at 0. Each time a new Counter is created, increment `total`. Add a static method `getTotal()` that returns the current count. Create 4 Counter instances and log the total.
What does `super` do in a subclass constructor and in a subclass method? What happens if you forget to call `super()` in a subclass constructor?
questions.sample_answer: In a subclass constructor, `super(args)` calls the parent class's constructor — it initialises the parent's properties on the new instance. You must call super() before using `this` in the subclass constructor. In a subclass method, `super.methodName()` calls the parent class's version of that method — useful when you want to extend (not fully replace) the parent's behaviour. If you forget `super()` in the constructor: JavaScript throws a ReferenceError saying you must call super before accessing `this`. The instance can't be created because the parent's setup hasn't run — the object isn't properly initialised.

Create a base class `Shape` with a method `getArea()` that returns 0. Create subclasses `Circle` (takes radius, area = π × r²) and `Rectangle` (takes width and height, area = w × h). Create an array with one Circle (radius 5) and one Rectangle (4 × 6). Use forEach to log each shape's area.
What is polymorphism? How does it work in the context of JavaScript classes and method overriding?
questions.sample_answer: Polymorphism means 'many forms' — the same method name produces different behaviour depending on which class the object belongs to. In JavaScript, when a subclass overrides a parent method, calling that method on the subclass instance runs the subclass version, not the parent's. This means you can write code that works with an array of mixed types: `shapes.forEach(s => console.log(s.getArea()))` — each shape calls its own getArea() automatically. The calling code doesn't need to know whether it's a Circle or Rectangle. This makes code extensible: you can add a new Triangle subclass later, and the forEach loop works with it automatically without modification.

Create a class `TaskManager` with a static method `createFromArray(arr)` that takes an array of task name strings and returns an array of task objects: `[{id: 1, name: 'Buy groceries', done: false}, ...]`. Call the static method with ['Buy groceries', 'Write code', 'Read book'] and log the result.
What is the difference between a static method and an instance method? When would you use each?
questions.sample_answer: An instance method is called on an instance (`myObj.doSomething()`) and has access to `this` — the specific object's data. A static method is called on the class itself (`MyClass.doSomething()`) and does NOT have access to any instance — there's no `this` pointing to a specific object. Use instance methods when the behaviour depends on the instance's data (e.g., `student.getGrade()` needs that student's score). Use static methods for utility operations related to the class but not tied to a specific instance: factory methods (`User.fromCSV(line)`), counters (`User.getCount()`), or helpers (`MathHelper.average(arr)`). A static method can't access instance properties because it doesn't know which instance you mean.

questions.prompt: Why does `getSongs()` in a Playlist class return `[...this.#songs]` instead of `this.#songs` directly? What problem does this solve?
questions.sample_answer: Returning `this.#songs` directly gives the caller a reference to the actual private array. They could then modify it externally — `playlist.getSongs().push('Hacked Song')` — and that modification would affect the private field, bypassing the class's controlled interface. The whole point of making it private is lost. Returning `[...this.#songs]` creates a shallow copy — a new array with the same elements. The caller can do whatever they want with the copy without affecting the original private array. This is defensive copying — it preserves encapsulation by ensuring the private state can only be changed through methods the class defines (like `addSong`).
